questions.q: Which description matches the CPU?
choices: The engine that interprets and executes instructions
Where program instructions and data are kept while the machine is running
The set of parallel wires that carries bits between components
The part of the computer that handles input and output devices
questions.explain: The CPU (processor) interprets and executes instructions. The other choices describe main memory, the system bus and the I/O subsystem.

questions.q: The fetch-and-execute cycle is also called the ______ cycle.
questions.explain: Fetch-and-execute cycle and instruction cycle are two names for the same thing.

questions.q: What are the three steps of the instruction cycle, in order?
choices: Fetch, decode, execute
Decode, fetch, execute
Fetch, execute, decode
Load, execute, store
questions.explain: The CPU fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it, then executes it, and repeats.

questions.q: Which of these are CPU responsibilities?
choices: Running the applications on the computer
Reading from and writing to memory
Switching between processes
Keeping data after the machine is powered off
questions.explain: The CPU runs applications and maintains system operations such as memory reads/writes and process switching. Keeping data with the power off is the job of disk (secondary storage).

questions.q: The system diagram has four major parts. Which of these is NOT one of the four?
choices: Cache
CPU
System bus
I/O subsystem
questions.explain: The four major parts are the CPU, main memory, the system bus and the I/O subsystem. Cache is a component inside the CPU box.

questions.q: The CPU in a typical personal computer is likely executing billions of instructions per second.
questions.explain: Modern PC CPUs execute billions of instructions per second.

questions.q: What does the Program Counter (PC) hold?
choices: The memory address of the next instruction to fetch
The instruction currently being decoded or executed
The result of the most recent ALU operation
The OpCode being sent to the ALU
questions.explain: The PC holds an address, namely where the next instruction is in memory. It does not hold the instruction itself.

questions.q: What does the Instruction Register (IR) hold?
choices: The actual instruction the CPU is currently decoding or executing
The memory address of the next instruction
The default address used when the machine boots
Operands and intermediate results used during computation
questions.explain: The IR holds the current instruction. The PC holds the next instruction's address, the reset vector is the boot address, and GPRs hold operands.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes fetching an instruction?
choices: Use the address in the PC, take the instruction stored there, place it in the IR, then increment the PC
Use the instruction in the IR, place its address in the PC, then increment the IR
Increment the PC, copy the PC into the IR, then read memory at the IR's address
Copy the PC into a GPR, send it through the ALU, then place the result in the IR
questions.explain: The CPU reaches out to the address stored in the PC, takes the instruction at that address, puts it in the IR, and then the PC increments.

questions.q: After an instruction is fetched, the PC is always updated by a simple increment.
questions.explain: The update may be a simple increment or something more complex, such as a branch or jump to a different address.

questions.q: What is the name of the default memory address the PC points to when the machine boots?
questions.explain: The reset vector is the PC's default address at boot. On most CPUs it is hardwired and part of the firmware.

questions.q: On most CPUs, where is the reset vector defined?
choices: It is hardwired into the machine as part of the firmware
The operating system writes it to main memory at shutdown
It is kept in L1 cache between power cycles
The user picks it the first time a program runs
questions.explain: The reset vector is hardwired and part of the firmware, which is built-in software that initializes the hardware.

questions.q: Firmware is built-in software that initializes the hardware. Give the common example of firmware (an acronym).
questions.explain: BIOS is the standard example of firmware. It holds things like the reset vector.

questions.q: Which of these are jobs of the Control Unit?
choices: Managing the fetch-and-execute cycle
Sending the address and the READ signal to memory during fetch
Parsing an instruction and generating the signals needed to execute it
Performing additions and value comparisons
Carrying out STORE instructions during execute
questions.explain: The CU manages the cycle, handles fetch, and decodes instructions into control signals. Arithmetic and comparisons belong to the ALU, and STORE belongs to the LSU.

questions.q: A program runs in sequence and the instruction at address 1000 has just been fetched. While that instruction is being decoded, what does the PC hold?
choices: The address of the instruction that follows the one at 1000
Address 1000
The instruction from address 1000
Nothing; the PC is cleared until execute finishes
questions.explain: The PC updates right after fetch. During decode and execute it already points to the next instruction, while the IR holds the current one.

questions.q: Why are registers faster to access than any other memory or storage?
choices: They are located directly in the CPU
They are non-volatile
They are much larger than main memory
They are reached through the system bus
questions.explain: Registers sit directly in the CPU, so the CPU can reach them without going out to memory.

questions.q: The Program Counter and the Instruction Register are both examples of:
choices: Special-purpose registers (SPRs)
General-purpose registers (GPRs)
Cache tiers
Controllers
questions.explain: SPRs have specific, dedicated purposes. The PC and IR are both SPRs.

questions.q: What do general-purpose registers (GPRs) hold?
choices: Operands, such as data values and intermediate results, used during computation
Only the address of the next instruction
Only the instruction currently being executed
Program code loaded from disk
questions.explain: GPRs hold operands for computation. The next-instruction address and the current instruction are held by the SPRs (PC and IR).

questions.q: Registers are the fastest storage. Why don't computers just use registers instead of main memory?
choices: Registers are significantly more expensive to produce
Registers take up space directly on the CPU
Registers require more power and generate more heat
Registers are slower than main memory
Registers are volatile and main memory is not
questions.explain: Registers cost more, use CPU space, and need more power and produce more heat. They are faster than main memory, and both registers and main memory are volatile.

questions.q: A CPU has 16 GPRs, each 32 bits wide. How many bytes of GPR storage is that in total?
questions.explain: 16 x 32 = 512 bits, and 512 / 8 = 64 bytes.

questions.q: A CPU has 32 GPRs, each 64 bits wide. How many bytes of GPR storage is that in total?
How many general-purpose registers do modern processors tend to have?
choices: 2 to 4
About one per megabyte of RAM
questions.explain: Modern processors tend to have 16 to 32 GPRs. Each GPR's size is determined by the architecture.

questions.q: Every GPR is 32 bits wide, no matter which CPU architecture it belongs to.
questions.explain: Each GPR's size is determined by the architecture.

questions.q: What does the ALU receive as input?
choices: Two operands from CPU registers, and an operation sent as a control signal based on the most recently decoded instruction
Two operands read straight from main memory, and an operation sent by the Program Counter
One operand from cache and a memory address from the address bus
The current instruction from the IR, which the ALU decodes by itself
questions.explain: Operands come from registers in the CPU. The operation is a control signal determined by the most recently decoded instruction, and decoding is the Control Unit's job.

questions.q: The ALU is a combinational circuit. What does that mean?
choices: It has no internal memory, and its output does not depend on any previous input
It stores its last result so it can use it in the next calculation
It combines the CPU and main memory into one unit
It can only update when the clock ticks
questions.explain: A combinational circuit's output depends only on its current inputs, so the same inputs always give the same output. Registers are the parts that hold values and update on clock ticks.

questions.q: Which of these operations are performed by the ALU?
choices: Addition and subtraction
Logical AND / OR
Value comparisons such as == and <
Loading a value from memory into a register
Fetching the next instruction
questions.explain: The ALU handles arithmetic, logical operations and comparisons. Loads go through the LSU, and fetch is handled by the Control Unit.

questions.q: In the example ALU's OpCode table (ADD 00, SUB 01, NOT 10, NEG 11), which operation does OpCode 01 select?
choices: SUB
ADD
NOT
NEG
questions.explain: 00 = ADD, 01 = SUB, 10 = NOT, 11 = NEG.

questions.q: In the example ALU (2-bit OpCode: ADD, SUB, NOT, NEG in order), what OpCode selects NEG?
questions.explain: The four codes go 00 ADD, 01 SUB, 10 NOT, 11 NEG.

questions.q: How many distinct operations can a 4-bit OpCode select?
questions.explain: An n-bit OpCode has 2^n values: 2^4 = 16. A 2-bit OpCode gives only 4, which is why modern CPUs use 4 to 8 bit OpCodes.

questions.q: In the example 8-bit ALU, A = 00000110, B = 00000110 and OpCode = 01. Which flag would you expect to be set?
choices: Zero
Negative
Overflow
None of the flags
questions.explain: 01 is SUB, so the result is 6 - 6 = 0 (00000000). A zero result sets the Zero flag.

questions.q: In the example 8-bit ALU, A = 00000101, B = 00000011 and OpCode = 00 (ADD). What is the 8-bit output, written in binary?
questions.explain: 5 + 3 = 8, which is 00001000 in 8 bits.

questions.q: The slides' ALU with 8-bit inputs and a 2-bit OpCode is typical of a modern CPU.
questions.explain: That ALU is only an example. A modern CPU would more likely use 64-bit inputs and outputs and a 4 to 8 bit OpCode.

questions.q: What are logic gates made from?
choices: Transistors, which are switches that control the flow of electrical current
Registers, which hold values between clock ticks
Small ALUs, each able to do one operation
Cache cells that store recently used bits
questions.explain: Transistors build logic gates, gates build the ALU, and the ALU performs operations like ADD and SUB.

questions.q: Which ordering goes from the smallest building block to the largest?
choices: Transistors, logic gates, ALU
Logic gates, transistors, ALU
ALU, logic gates, transistors
Transistors, ALU, logic gates
questions.explain: Transistors make up logic gates, and logic gates perform the ALU's operations.

questions.q: Which of these are basic logic gates?
choices: AND
OR
NOT
XOR
LOAD
PUSH
questions.explain: AND, OR, NOT and XOR are the gates behind binary manipulation. LOAD and PUSH are memory operations handled by the LSU.

questions.q: Which CPU component carries out a STORE instruction?
choices: Load-Store Unit (LSU)
Arithmetic/Logic Unit (ALU)
Program Counter
Clock
questions.explain: The LSU handles memory operations: loading values from memory and storing values to memory.

questions.q: LOAD and STORE are carried out by the ALU, since they move data between registers and memory.
questions.explain: Memory operations are not arithmetic or logical, so they do not need the ALU. They go through the LSU.

questions.q: Fetching an instruction reads from memory. Which unit handles it, and why?
choices: The Control Unit, because fetch is not part of executing an instruction
The LSU, because every memory read goes through the LSU
The ALU, because the PC must be incremented
The disk controller, because instructions are stored on disk
questions.explain: Fetch is the exception to 'memory accesses go through the LSU'. It is not part of an execution, so the Control Unit does it.

questions.q: Which of these are usually handled through the LSU?
choices: LOAD
STORE
PUSH
POP
Instruction fetch
ADD
questions.explain: Regular memory accesses (LOAD, STORE, PUSH, POP) go through the LSU. Fetch belongs to the CU, and ADD is done by the ALU.

questions.q: In the system diagram, the LSU connects directly to which two components?
choices: Cache and the register file
The PC and the IR
The ALU and the clock
The disk controller and the NIC
questions.explain: The LSU links up to the cache and into the register file. Values it loads end up in registers.

questions.q: When are registers allowed to update?
choices: Only when the clock ticks, on the edge of the clock signal
At any time the CPU's logic changes
Only when the system bus is idle
Only after the program finishes
questions.explain: The logic inside the CPU may change at any time, but registers only update on a clock tick (edge).

questions.q: What form does the CPU clock signal usually take?
choices: A square wave that alternates between high and low voltage
A sine wave whose frequency follows the workload
A single pulse sent once at boot
A counter value stored in the PC
questions.explain: The clock is a repeating time signal, usually a square wave alternating between high and low voltage.

questions.q: In what unit is clock speed usually measured? (Give the unit name or its abbreviation.)
questions.explain: Clock speed is generally measured in gigahertz. 3 GHz means 3 billion clock cycles per second.

questions.q: A CPU runs at 2 GHz. How long is one clock cycle, in nanoseconds?
questions.explain: 2 GHz is 2 x 10^9 cycles per second, so one cycle lasts 1 / (2 x 10^9) s = 0.5 ns.

questions.q: Why does overclocking (raising the clock speed) increase performance?
choices: More cycles per second means more register updates per second
It adds more general-purpose registers
It makes main memory non-volatile
It lets the ALU remember earlier results
questions.explain: Each clock cycle is a chance for registers to update. More cycles per second means more updates, so more work gets done.

questions.q: In the system diagram, which components are connected to the clock?
choices: The register file and the ALU
Main memory and the system bus
The USB controller and the disk controller
The cache and the LSU only
questions.explain: The clock has dashed connections to the register file and the ALU, synchronizing activity inside the CPU.

questions.q: What is main memory?
choices: Where the computer stores program instructions and data while the machine is running
Where the computer keeps files permanently after power-off
Small, fast storage inside the CPU for recently used data
The set of registers contained in the CPU
questions.explain: Main memory holds instructions and data while the machine runs. The other choices describe disk, cache and the register file.

questions.q: Which events cause the data held in main memory to disappear?
choices: The program that owns it terminates
The machine is shut down
The program or machine crashes
Power is removed
The file is saved to disk
questions.explain: Main memory is temporary and volatile, so termination, shutdown, crashes and power loss all wipe it. Saving to disk is how you keep data.

questions.q: What does 'random-access' mean in random-access memory (RAM)?
choices: Any address can be reached instantly without stepping past other locations, so access time is the same everywhere
Data is placed at random addresses to spread out wear
Access time depends on how far the address is from the start of memory
The CPU picks a random address on each read
questions.explain: Random-access means any address can be accessed instantly, without traversal. As a result, access time is the same for all RAM data.

questions.q: A program runs faster if its data is placed at lower addresses in RAM.
questions.explain: RAM access time is the same for every address, so program speed does not depend on where data sits in RAM.

questions.q: How is main memory organized?
choices: As a linear array of bytes, each with its own address
As three tiers called L1, L2 and L3
As a set of 16 to 32 general-purpose registers
As spinning magnetic plates divided into tracks
questions.explain: Main memory is a linear array of bytes, each with its own address. The CPU uses that address to reach the data.

questions.q: When data is read from main memory, where does the CPU put it?
choices: In the appropriate register (IR, GPRs, etc.) or in cache
Inside the ALU's internal memory
In the disk controller
Back in main memory at a new address
questions.explain: Data sent from main memory goes into the right register or into cache. The ALU has no internal memory.

questions.q: Using 1 GB = 2^30 bytes, 8 GB of RAM equals 2^n bytes. What is n?
How much RAM do most modern personal computers have?
choices: 8 to 64 GB
20 to 60 MB
64 bytes
256 GB to 4 TB
questions.explain: Most modern PCs have 8 to 64 GB of RAM, and some have 1 TB or more. 20-60 MB is typical total cache, and 256 GB to 4 TB is typical disk.

questions.q: You are partway through a game and have not saved. Where is your current progress stored?
choices: Main memory
Disk memory
The reset vector
The disk controller
questions.explain: Active data, such as unsaved document changes or game progress, lives in main memory until it is saved.

questions.q: What is the system bus?
choices: A collection of pathways (parallel wires) that carry bits between the processor and other parts of the computer
A special-purpose register that holds the next address
A type of cache shared by all CPU cores
The controller that connects USB devices to the CPU
questions.explain: The bus lets the CPU, main memory and I/O devices communicate. Without it, each component would be an isolated box.

questions.q: Which bus carries the command being performed, such as READ or WRITE?
choices: Control bus
Address bus
Data bus
Instruction bus
questions.explain: Address bus = where, data bus = what, control bus = which action.

questions.q: Which bus carries the location the CPU will read from or write to?
choices: Address bus
Data bus
Control bus
Clock bus
questions.explain: The address bus carries the address of the data being read or written.

questions.q: Which bus carries the actual value being transferred between components?
choices: Data bus
Address bus
Control bus
Register bus
questions.explain: The data bus carries the data value, for example an instruction coming back during fetch.

questions.q: Which of these happen on the system bus during the fetch phase?
choices: The address from the PC is placed on the address bus
READ is placed on the control bus
The instruction at that address comes back to the CPU on the data bus
WRITE is placed on the control bus
The ALU's result is placed on the data bus
questions.explain: During fetch the CU puts the PC's address on the address bus and READ on the control bus, and memory returns the instruction on the data bus.

questions.q: The decode phase normally uses the system bus to send signals to the other CPU components.
questions.explain: Decode happens inside the CPU. The CU decodes the instruction in the IR and signals the other CPU components without using the system bus.

questions.q: An instruction writes a value to memory. What is on each bus?
choices: Address bus: the destination address; Control bus: WRITE; Data bus: the value being written
Address bus: the value being written; Control bus: WRITE; Data bus: the destination address
Address bus: the destination address; Control bus: READ; Data bus: the value being written
Address bus: the address in the PC; Control bus: WRITE; Data bus: the instruction in the IR
questions.explain: For a write, the data goes on the data bus, WRITE on the control bus, and the destination address on the address bus.

questions.q: Bus activity during fetch is handled by the ____, and memory reads/writes during execute are handled by the ____.
choices: CU; LSU
LSU; CU
ALU; LSU
LSU; LSU
questions.explain: Fetch is not part of an execution, so the Control Unit handles it. Memory accesses during execution go through the Load-Store Unit.

questions.q: What is cache memory?
choices: Small, fast memory in the CPU (or nearby) that stores recent and/or frequently used data
Large, slow, permanent storage reached through a controller
The register that holds the current instruction
The linear array of bytes that holds every running program
questions.explain: Cache is small, fast memory close to the CPU that keeps recent or frequently used data.

questions.q: How does cache improve performance?
choices: It reduces the number of requests to slower main memory, avoiding the delay each request causes
It raises the clock speed of the CPU
It makes main memory non-volatile
It lets the ALU skip the decode phase
questions.explain: Every trip to main memory adds a delay. Keeping important data in cache cuts down those trips.

questions.q: Which cache level is the smallest and fastest?
choices: L1
L2
L3
All three are the same size and speed
questions.explain: L1 is the smallest and fastest, and L3 is the largest and slowest.

questions.q: L3 cache is the largest and slowest of the three cache levels.
questions.explain: Going from L3 to L2 to L1, each tier is smaller and faster.

questions.q: Unlike main memory, cache keeps its contents when the power is removed.
questions.explain: Like main memory, cache is temporary and volatile.

questions.q: About how much total cache do current consumer devices generally have?
choices: 20 to 60 MB
8 to 64 GB
64 bytes
256 GB to 4 TB
questions.explain: Consumer devices generally have 20 to 60 MB of total cache, roughly 20 to 60 million bytes.

questions.q: Which ordering goes from fastest to slowest?
choices: Registers, L1 cache, L2 cache, L3 cache, main memory, disk
L1 cache, registers, L2 cache, L3 cache, disk, main memory
Registers, L3 cache, L2 cache, L1 cache, main memory, disk
Main memory, registers, L1 cache, L2 cache, L3 cache, disk
questions.explain: Registers are fastest. L1 is faster than L2, which is faster than L3. Main memory is slower than cache, and disk is slowest.

questions.q: Why must cache be managed effectively?
choices: It is significantly smaller than main memory, and poor cache management can tank performance
It is permanent, so mistakes are saved forever
It is slower than main memory, so it should be avoided
It is reached only through the disk controller
questions.explain: Cache is fast but small, so hardware and software are designed to use it well. Poor management can tank performance.

questions.q: In the system diagram, which CPU unit connects directly to the cache?
choices: Load-Store Unit (LSU)
Arithmetic/Logic Unit (ALU)
Control Unit (CU)
Clock
questions.explain: Memory loads and stores pass through the LSU, so the LSU is the unit connected to the cache.

questions.q: What is the I/O subsystem responsible for?
choices: Handling all input and output devices
Decoding instructions in the IR
Holding program instructions while they run
Synchronizing register updates
questions.explain: The I/O subsystem handles input and output devices, including disk storage.

questions.q: The CPU, main memory and system bus are enough for computation to happen. Why is an I/O subsystem still needed?
choices: Without it we could not give the computer commands or see its results
Without it the CPU could not perform arithmetic
Without it the PC could not find the reset vector
Without it main memory could not be addressed
questions.explain: We need a way to interact with the system by giving inputs and receiving outputs.

questions.q: An integrated graphics adapter is not an I/O device, because it is built into the computer rather than external.
questions.explain: I/O does not mean external. Integrated graphics adapters are I/O devices and the machine treats them that way.

questions.q: Which of these are I/O devices?
choices: A graphics card
A network interface card built into the motherboard
Disk memory (secondary storage)
A keyboard
The ALU
L2 cache
questions.explain: Graphics adapters, NICs (even built-in ones), disk and keyboards are all I/O devices. The ALU and cache are parts of the CPU.

questions.q: What is a controller?
choices: A hardware interface that lets the system send signals to a device without needing to understand the device's exact behavior
The CPU component that manages the fetch-and-execute cycle
Software in the OS that stores files permanently
A bus line that carries READ and WRITE commands
questions.explain: With a controller in between, the CPU only needs to know what to tell a device, not how the device works. (The CPU component in the second choice is the Control Unit, which is a different thing.)

questions.q: The CPU communicates with I/O devices directly, without any intermediary.
questions.explain: Communication with I/O devices goes through a controller.

questions.q: Which of these are both an I/O device and a controller?
choices: Graphics adapter
Network interface card (NIC)
USB controller
Disk controller
questions.explain: Graphics adapters and NICs are both I/O devices and controllers. The USB and disk controllers are separate from the devices they serve.

questions.q: In the system diagram, the keyboard and mouse reach the system bus through which component?
choices: USB controller
Graphics adapter
NIC
Disk controller
questions.explain: The USB controller interfaces with the whole array of USB devices, including the keyboard and mouse in the diagram.

questions.q: What does a network interface card (NIC) do?
choices: Lets the computer send and receive data through Ethernet, Wi-Fi, etc.
Produces graphic output for display devices
Stores data permanently on spinning plates
Synchronizes register updates inside the CPU
questions.explain: The NIC handles network communication. Nearly all modern computers have one built into the motherboard, and it is still an I/O device.

questions.q: Secondary storage is also commonly called:
choices: Disk memory
Main memory
Cache memory
Register memory
questions.explain: Secondary storage and disk memory are interchangeable terms for storage that keeps data indefinitely.

questions.q: Which pair of words describes disk memory?
choices: Permanent and non-volatile
Temporary and volatile
Permanent and volatile
Temporary and non-volatile
questions.explain: Disk memory survives program termination, crashes and power-off. Main memory and cache are temporary and volatile.

questions.q: How does a Hard Disk Drive (HDD) store data?
choices: On spinning magnetic plates
Via trapped electrical charges
As software-defined storage in a virtual machine
In the CPU's register file
questions.explain: HDDs use spinning magnetic plates. SSDs use trapped electrical charges.

questions.q: How does a Solid State Drive (SSD) store data?
choices: Via trapped electrical charges
On spinning magnetic plates
On rotating floppy disks
In L3 cache
questions.explain: SSDs store data as trapped electrical charges, with no spinning parts.

questions.q: What is a Virtual Hard Disk (VHD)?
choices: Software-defined storage used in virtual machines and cloud computing
A hard disk with extra magnetic plates
A USB drive used to move data between devices
A section of main memory that acts like a disk
questions.explain: A VHD is software-defined storage used in VMs and the cloud. USB drives and SD cards are removable storage.

questions.q: In the system diagram, where is disk memory?
choices: In the I/O subsystem, behind the disk controller
Inside main memory, next to the Data section
Inside the CPU, next to the cache
Directly on the system bus with no controller
questions.explain: Disk is treated as an I/O device. It sits in the I/O subsystem and is reached through the disk controller.

questions.q: Compared with main memory, disk storage is:
choices: Slower and cheaper, and built for large amounts of permanent storage
Faster and more expensive
Faster and cheaper, but volatile
Slower and more expensive, but smaller
questions.explain: Just as main memory is slower and cheaper than registers, disk is slower and cheaper than main memory. It trades access time for large, cheap, permanent storage.

questions.q: Using 1 GB = 2^30 bytes and 1 TB = 2^40 bytes, how many GB are in 1 TB?
You are editing a document you saved an hour ago, and the power goes out. What happens?
choices: The changes since the last save are lost because they were in volatile main memory, but the saved version on disk survives
Everything survives, because main memory is non-volatile
Both the unsaved changes and the saved file are lost
The unsaved changes survive in cache, but the saved file is lost
questions.explain: Active data lives in main memory, which is volatile. Saved data is on disk, which is non-volatile.

questions.q: Where does the term 'disk' in disk memory come from?
choices: Early storage devices such as hard disks and floppy disks used magnetized rotating disks
Disk stands for an acronym for 'Data In Storage Kernel'
All modern storage devices still contain a spinning disk
RAM chips are shaped like disks
questions.explain: The name comes from early magnetic rotating disks. Today 'disk' can mean an HDD, SSD, VHD or removable storage.

questions.q: How much disk storage might a modern computer have?
choices: 256 GB to 4 TB
8 to 64 GB
20 to 60 MB
64 bytes
questions.explain: Modern computers might have 256 GB to 4 TB of disk storage, far more than RAM (8-64 GB) or cache (20-60 MB).

questions.q: A user launches a program. Before the CPU can fetch its instructions, where must the program's code be?
choices: Loaded from disk into main memory
Left on disk, because the CPU fetches instructions directly from the disk controller
Copied entirely into the general-purpose registers
Written into the reset vector
questions.explain: Any time you run a program, its code is loaded into main memory so the CPU can access it.

questions.q: For a LOAD instruction, which unit handles each phase?
choices: Fetch: CU; Decode: CU; Execute: LSU
Fetch: LSU; Decode: CU; Execute: LSU
Fetch: CU; Decode: ALU; Execute: LSU
Fetch: LSU; Decode: ALU; Execute: ALU
questions.explain: The CU fetches and decodes every instruction. Because LOAD is a memory access during execution, the LSU carries it out.

questions.q: The current instruction adds two values already held in registers. Which of these does its execute phase use?
choices: The ALU
General-purpose registers
The Load-Store Unit
The system bus
questions.explain: The operands come from GPRs, the ALU adds them, and the result goes back to a register. No memory access is needed, so the LSU and system bus are not used.

questions.q: How does the ALU know that the current instruction is an ADD?
choices: The Control Unit decodes the instruction and sends the operation (OpCode) to the ALU as a control signal
The ALU remembers which operation it performed last
The LSU loads the operation from cache
The PC sends the operation along with the next address
questions.explain: The ALU is combinational and has no memory. Its operation is a control signal determined by the most recently decoded instruction.

questions.q: While one instruction is processed, the PC update, the IR load and the write of the result register all take effect on clock ticks.
questions.explain: Registers only update when the clock ticks, and the PC, IR and GPRs are all registers.
